sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title, Lehiste et al. 2005 'Meadow Mari Prosody' (Glottolog 110928), already held with a text from the 2026-09-16 download (kirj.ee open PDF, DOI 10.3176/lu.2005.2s); re-read pp.13-14, 17-30, 64-71, 91-94 and logged in It is squarely about word stress in this language (Meadow = Eastern Mari, mhr) and REFINES the catalog's weight-hedged coding: the received rule 'last full vowel, else initial' appears only as the reported common claim (p.14, quoting Kangasmaa-Minn 1998:224 verbatim on p.20; Itkonen/Kiparsky on p.21), while the authors' own 8-speaker acoustic data show placement is not fixed (speakers disagreed on 16/58 disyllables and 7/17 trisyllables; a Bashkortostan speaker favoured initial stress), at least one stress minimal pair exists (šérge 'dear' ~ šergé 'comb'), duration is the main cue, and all-schwa words are initially stressed (pp.64-65, 68-69, 93-94). This contradicts Sebeok & Ingemann 1961's 'stress is not phonemic' assumption in the deciding quote but not the coded rule; it is the best first-hand support for the 'hedged' flag rather than a replacement deciding source for the placement rule (Kangasmaa-Minn 1998 / Riese et al. 2022 / Vaysman 2009, already in the record, remain the rule statements). Chapter 2 also supplies verified verbatim secondary quotes (Collinder 1965:42-43, Ristinen 1960:259, Karmazin 1936, Zorina 1982:46, Kuklin 2003) usable in the bibliography. Nothing left to acquire for this item; for the session was exhausted so no additional titles beyond the item list were checked online.

new_statements.reading: First-hand instrumental evidence from 8 speakers that Meadow Mari word stress is lexically variable rather than positionally fixed, with real inter- and intra-speaker disagreement, that it can be contrastive (one minimal pair), and that all-reduced-vowel words take initial stress. It supports the weight basis (full vs reduced vowel) and, strongly, the 'hedged' flag; it does not itself state the 'last full vowel, else initial' rule from its own data but reports it as the received claim (Kangasmaa-Minn 1998:224, quoted verbatim on p.20).

sources.quote: Normally, stress — indicated here by bold italics — falls upon the last full vowel of the word, e.g. ila '(s)he lives' and tolə-t 'they come'. It is a general tendency, almost a universal, that the imperative strives to distinguish itself from other moods. In Mari this manifests itself by the stress leaping one syllable to the left so that — most bases being bisyllabic — the stress falls on the first syllable. The leap of stress onto the first syllable, in its turn, induces reduction of the vowel in the second syllable, which is now without stress.
sources.note: Glottocode assignment is the compiler mapping of the paper's 'central subdialect of Mari (Cheremis)' (contrasted with 'Western' forms, p. 37 sec. 3.1) to Eastern/Meadow Mari; the paper gives no code. System stated: stress on the last full (non-reduced) vowel; reduced ə never stressed (p. 38: 'ə is unstressed, while a is stressed'); imperative/connegative marked by stress retracting one syllable leftward to the first syllable with reduction of the now-unstressed final vowel (a > e, ə > zero). sources.quote: Stress in Mari is not bound to a certain syllable, but as a general rule falls on the last full vowel of the word. Full vowels are all vowels apart from a) the vowel ы /ə̑/ and b) unstressed е, о, and ӧ in word-final position. (These vowels are almost always unstressed in the final position. Certain words and suffixes exist that contain stressed variants of these vowels in the final position, these will be discussed as they occur.) In word-final position unstressed е, о, and ӧ are slightly reduced in pronunciation and alternate with ы when a suffix is added, e.g., тудо /tudo/ 'he/she/it' – тудым /tudə̑m/ 'him/her/it (accusative)'. [...] If a word contains only reduced vowels (only ы, or ы with е, о, or ӧ in word-final position), stress falls on the first syllable.

sources.quote: On the basis of our limited corpus we assume that stress is not phonemic and, accordingly, do not mark it in the texts. In words with the following vowel configurations two stress patterns are possible: [table of five final-vowel / preceding-vowel configurations, e.g. pire ~ pire 'wolf', korno ~ korno 'road', kidsam ~ kidsam 'his hand (acc.)', pugalmo ~ pugalmo 'cone'] In such words, stress may fall on either the final vowel — although a few final morphemes, such as -kan 'if,' never carry stress — or on the nearest preceding "full" vowel. Thus words with vowel configurations 1, 2, 3, or 4 may be stressed on the penult. Words with vowel configuration 5 may be stressed on the nearest preceding /i, e, a, ö, ü, o, u/ or, if none of these occurs within the word, on the first vowel. Which of the two possible stress patterns occurs in the flow of speech would seem to depend on overriding patterns of intonation, rhythm, and the like. Words which do not contain this vowel harmony, are always stressed on the last vowel. Russian loanwords often retain Russian stress patterns.
